author: Torta
subject: Open Letter to Blizzard Entertainment
content_md:
Dear Blizzard Entertainment,

We're Turtle WoW, a group of fans who love World of Warcraft and share a lifelong dream of contributing to its development. Mysteries of Azeroth, our content expansion, is a collective effort of our community members: writers, developers, 3D-modellers, composers, voice actors, game designers, artists, and radio DJs, each pouring their soul and skills into creating an environment where others can experience the vision we all share through expanding and adding onto the universe you have created.

During the seven years we've been online, we have worked towards finding the right recipe to add an element of replayability to the natural progression of an MMO world. Every update brings fresh areas to explore, new ways to engage with the game, and levelling challenges that require players to approach the experience with creativity and strategy, while the hard‑earned progress they've fought for remains valuable as the game continues to evolve. The response from our community has been nothing short of positive and heart‑warming. Our players have consistently expressed that Mysteries of Azeroth "feels like a home that always welcomes players back".

Many successful games have a modding community. It is a part of gaming culture and a testament to the game's quality, and the community's passion. The World of Warcraft modding community is flourishing, and as more tools become available, it will only continue to grow. Everything your devoted fans create enriches the game universe with diverse perspectives and innovative ideas. Your storytelling has inspired this creativity, and we hope that Blizzard embraces fan‑driven content as its own legacy, rather than alienate this passionate community.

Unfortunately, unlike other studios, Blizzard does not yet have a framework that allows projects like ours to operate without risking legal conflict. With that in mind, we respectfully ask that Blizzard consider establishing a formal ecosystem for licensing fan‑run community servers.

On behalf of our community, we can say that all players would be deeply grateful if you would consider working with fan communities like ours to create a clear, lawful pathway for building upon the legacy of the World of Warcraft universe, with your blessing. By fostering an ecosystem for modders to run their own community servers, Blizzard can continue to oversee and control its progress while encouraging fan-driven innovation. This approach would not only enhance the gameplay experience, but also strengthen the bonds between developers and players, ensuring that World of Warcraft remains a true home for everyone who loves it.

 **Other successful studios have shown how rewarding a well‑structured community‑server ecosystem can be:**

- **Daybreak Game Company** provides legal permission for Project 1999, a private server that faithfully recreates the classic EverQuest experience. The partnership is confirmed by an [official statement](https://www.everquest.com/news/project-1999-daybreak) and discussed openly on the [project's forums](https://www.project1999.com/forums/showthread.php?t=191146).

- **Rockstar Games / GTA V** partnered with the [FiveM](https://fivem.net/) platform that enables community‑run multiplayer servers that use Rockstar’s GTA V engine while adhering to a licensing agreement that permits custom game modes, role‑playing worlds, and user‑generated content. Over [1 million](https://content.htnetwork.one/how-many-people-play-fivem/) concurrent players have been reported on FiveM servers, illustrating how a major publisher can safely coexist with a fan‑driven ecosystem while maintaining control over the core IP.

- **NCSoft** granted a license to the [Homecoming](https://forums.homecomingservers.com/topic/47223-ncsoft-homecoming-license-announcement/) private‑server project for **City of Heroes**, allowing the community to continue operating the MMO under a clear legal agreement that protects the IP and player accounts.

- **Bethesda** has long supported Skyrim mods, providing official tools that have kept the game vibrant for years.

- **Valve** opened the Source engine to the public, a decision that birthed enduring titles such as Counter‑Strike and Team Fortress 2.

- **Epic Games** introduced Creative Mode in Fortnite, turning players into co‑creators and dramatically boosting engagement. Epic also released the source code for [Unreal Tournament 99](https://www.epicgames.com/unrealtournament) to the community, allowing fans to continue development, produce new mods, and distribute classic builds through sites like oldunreal.com, thereby demonstrating that a major publisher can safely coexist with a fan‑run ecosystem.

- **Microsoft / Mojang** allows third‑party servers such as Hypixel, Mineplex, and many others to host multiplayer experiences built on the Minecraft engine. These servers operate under a clear licensing regime, generate massive player engagement, and extend the life of the core product while remaining fully compliant with Microsoft’s IP policies.

- **EA / Star Wars Battlefront II** cooperated with the community project [Kyber](https://forums.ea.com/discussions/star-wars-battlefront-2-en/hacks-fixed/12096261) to fix server‑side exploits, and its lead engineer later joined EA itself. Although no formal licensing announcement exists, this cooperation illustrates how a publisher and a fan‑run server can work together on security and stability.
These examples illustrate that, when a clear licensing framework and technical safeguards are in place, fan‑run servers can extend a franchise's lifespan, fuel low‑cost innovation, and strengthen the brand, all while respecting the publisher's intellectual‑property and security requirements.

 **Why it matters to Blizzard?**

A licensed framework for fan-run servers would extend World of Warcraft's active audience by bringing back players who have drifted away from the official game in search of niche experiences that mainstream releases can't accommodate. Community‑crafted mods fill those gaps, offering gameplay that appeals to smaller, passionate audiences. This not only keeps the overall player base larger and more diverse, but also gives Blizzard a source of successful concepts that can be identified and integrated into future official content.

We are open to any licensing structure that fits Blizzard's risk‑management and financial guidelines. Should Blizzard wish to move forward, we stand ready to adapt and meet whatever technical, security and data‑privacy standards you require.

 **Turtle WoW Community**

For the past seven years our players have poured countless hours into building characters and stories that make Turtle WoW feel like a living, ever‑changing world. Those memories and progress are priceless to us and to the people who call our servers home. A licensing framework would give them a permanent, protected home, so every character and memory can continue to live on without the fear of being lost.

We look forward to the day you embrace this opportunity and would welcome the chance to begin a dialogue, offering any support needed to bring this program to life.

Thank you for considering our ideas. We hope to find a resolution that will be best for the game and its gamers.

 **[[email protected]](https://forum.turtlecraft.gg/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#84e7ebeaf0e5e7f0c4f0f1f6f0e8e1e7f6e5e2f0aae3e3)**
Turtle WoW Team

author: Escaton1
subject: Re: Open Letter to Blizzard Entertainment
content_md:
I'm sure I'm not the only one in that situation, but I can safely say that Turtle WoW as a server did not remove me from the Blizzard customer base, and therefore didn't "steal" profit from Blizzard.

I have close to 15 years of WoW subscription in total, and I have played WoW and WoW classic before **and** after Turtle WoW (I stopped playing turtle some times two years ago and then went to play Season of Discovery). My point being that Turtle WoW doesn't need to be seen as a competitor but rather as a different experience to the retail servers, there are things that players can prefer in one version or the other, and that is entirely fair.

Would Blizzard offer an experience like that of Turtle WoW, I would have no issue paying a monthly sub to experience it. This is why a cooperation between Blizzard and Turtle WoW, or even other servers offering their own experience would be a good thing for all involved

author: Allwynd01
subject: Re: Open Letter to Blizzard Entertainment
content_md:
For me this raises a few questions:

 1. Turtle WoW now gets financial support from players who purchase things from the store. How will that continue if this goes through?

 2. Blizzard's WoW is full of many questionable changes in terms of story, characters, the way in Classic they change Male/Female for Body Type 1/Body Type 2 and many things like that. Turtle WoW doesn't have such things and I can't imagine how Blizzard will not force Turtle WoW to have "DEI" in order to exist if this ever becomes a reality. I personally disapprove of such "philosophies" in games and avoid playing them so if Turtle WoW becomes DEI-compatible, I will be playing on another Vanilla server.

 3. Overall I think this will never happen, because Blizzard are greedy and arrogant, they want to be making all the money and they hate it when someone steals their thunder. Only over their dead body they will endorse a 3rd party modder project that is objectively better than all they've done (save for Vanilla in 2004-2006).

When I started reading this message, I got flashbacks of Nostalrius bending the knee to Blizzard and then they shut down. Some people like to say that Nostalrius are the reason why WoW Classic exists, but I doubt that. It's just Blizzard had a momentary experience of clarity and saw that unless they capitalize on the old school vanilla fad that everyone is chasing, they are actively denying themselves that piece of the pie. Now they realize that Vanilla+ is the next path forward, but I don't believe that they will endorse private server projects under their wing, and as I mentioned above, if it happens by some massive fluke, the requirements and restrictions on them will be so horrible that you're better off running a PIRATE private server that's not endorsed and running the risk of being sought after by the law instead if you want creative freedom.

I hope this doesn't end up being Nostalrius 2.0 where Turtle WoW buckle and agree to what Blizzard wants, because nothing in the message indicates that they intend on continuing as-is if Blizzard refuse this proposition. To me sounds more like a desperate plea from Turtle WoW "please don't destroy us, we can be friends". I like Turtle WoW and will be unhappy if it's gone, but this message reads only this way to me.

author: Hanhazine001
subject: Re: Open Letter to Blizzard Entertainment
content_md:
> **Torta wrote: Fri Oct 17, 2025 1:49 pm**
> Dear Blizzard Entertainment,
>
>  We're Turtle WoW, a group of fans who love World of Warcraft and share a lifelong dream of contributing to its development. Mysteries of Azeroth, our content expansion, is a collective effort of our community members: writers, developers, 3D-modellers, composers, voice actors, game designers, artists, and radio DJs, each pouring their soul and skills into creating an environment where others can experience the vision we all share through expanding and adding onto the universe you have created.
>
>  During the seven years we've been online, we have worked towards finding the right recipe to add an element of replayability to the natural progression of an MMO world. Every update brings fresh areas to explore, new ways to engage with the game, and levelling challenges that require players to approach the experience with creativity and strategy, while the hard‑earned progress they've fought for remains valuable as the game continues to evolve. The response from our community has been nothing short of positive and heart‑warming. Our players have consistently expressed that Mysteries of Azeroth "feels like a home that always welcomes players back".
>
>  Many successful games have a modding community. It is a part of gaming culture and a testament to the game's quality, and the community's passion. The World of Warcraft modding community is flourishing, and as more tools become available, it will only continue to grow. Everything your devoted fans create enriches the game universe with diverse perspectives and innovative ideas. Your storytelling has inspired this creativity, and we hope that Blizzard embraces fan‑driven content as its own legacy, rather than alienate this passionate community.
>
>  Unfortunately, unlike other studios, Blizzard does not yet have a framework that allows projects like ours to operate without risking legal conflict. With that in mind, we respectfully ask that Blizzard consider establishing a formal ecosystem for licensing fan‑run community servers.
>
>  On behalf of our community, we can say that all players would be deeply grateful if you would consider working with fan communities like ours to create a clear, lawful pathway for building upon the legacy of the World of Warcraft universe, with your blessing. By fostering an ecosystem for modders to run their own community servers, Blizzard can continue to oversee and control its progress while encouraging fan-driven innovation. This approach would not only enhance the gameplay experience, but also strengthen the bonds between developers and players, ensuring that World of Warcraft remains a true home for everyone who loves it.
>
>  **Other successful studios have shown how rewarding a well‑structured community‑server ecosystem can be:**
>
> - **Daybreak Game Company** provides legal permission for Project 1999, a private server that faithfully recreates the classic EverQuest experience. The partnership is confirmed by an [official statement](https://www.everquest.com/news/project-1999-daybreak) and discussed openly on the [project's forums](https://www.project1999.com/forums/showthread.php?t=191146).
>
> - **Rockstar Games / GTA V** partnered with the [FiveM](https://fivem.net/) platform that enables community‑run multiplayer servers that use Rockstar’s GTA V engine while adhering to a licensing agreement that permits custom game modes, role‑playing worlds, and user‑generated content. Over [1 million](https://content.htnetwork.one/how-many-people-play-fivem/) concurrent players have been reported on FiveM servers, illustrating how a major publisher can safely coexist with a fan‑driven ecosystem while maintaining control over the core IP.
>
> - **NCSoft** granted a license to the [Homecoming](https://forums.homecomingservers.com/topic/47223-ncsoft-homecoming-license-announcement/) private‑server project for **City of Heroes**, allowing the community to continue operating the MMO under a clear legal agreement that protects the IP and player accounts.
>
> - **Bethesda** has long supported Skyrim mods, providing official tools that have kept the game vibrant for years.
>
> - **Valve** opened the Source engine to the public, a decision that birthed enduring titles such as Counter‑Strike and Team Fortress 2.
>
> - **Epic Games** introduced Creative Mode in Fortnite, turning players into co‑creators and dramatically boosting engagement. Epic also released the source code for [Unreal Tournament 99](https://www.epicgames.com/unrealtournament) to the community, allowing fans to continue development, produce new mods, and distribute classic builds through sites like oldunreal.com, thereby demonstrating that a major publisher can safely coexist with a fan‑run ecosystem.
>
> - **Microsoft / Mojang** allows third‑party servers such as Hypixel, Mineplex, and many others to host multiplayer experiences built on the Minecraft engine. These servers operate under a clear licensing regime, generate massive player engagement, and extend the life of the core product while remaining fully compliant with Microsoft’s IP policies.
>
> - **EA / Star Wars Battlefront II** cooperated with the community project [Kyber](https://forums.ea.com/discussions/star-wars-battlefront-2-en/hacks-fixed/12096261) to fix server‑side exploits, and its lead engineer later joined EA itself. Although no formal licensing announcement exists, this cooperation illustrates how a publisher and a fan‑run server can work together on security and stability.
>   These examples illustrate that, when a clear licensing framework and technical safeguards are in place, fan‑run servers can extend a franchise's lifespan, fuel low‑cost innovation, and strengthen the brand, all while respecting the publisher's intellectual‑property and security requirements.
>
>  **Why it matters to Blizzard?**
>
>  A licensed framework for fan-run servers would extend World of Warcraft's active audience by bringing back players who have drifted away from the official game in search of niche experiences that mainstream releases can't accommodate. Community‑crafted mods fill those gaps, offering gameplay that appeals to smaller, passionate audiences. This not only keeps the overall player base larger and more diverse, but also gives Blizzard a source of successful concepts that can be identified and integrated into future official content.
>
>  We are open to any licensing structure that fits Blizzard's risk‑management and financial guidelines. Should Blizzard wish to move forward, we stand ready to adapt and meet whatever technical, security and data‑privacy standards you require.
>
>  **Turtle WoW Community**
>
>  For the past seven years our players have poured countless hours into building characters and stories that make Turtle WoW feel like a living, ever‑changing world. Those memories and progress are priceless to us and to the people who call our servers home. A licensing framework would give them a permanent, protected home, so every character and memory can continue to live on without the fear of being lost.
>
>  We look forward to the day you embrace this opportunity and would welcome the chance to begin a dialogue, offering any support needed to bring this program to life.
>
>  Thank you for considering our ideas. We hope to find a resolution that will be best for the game and its gamers.
>
>  **[[email protected]](https://forum.turtlecraft.gg/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#d6b5b9b8a2b7b5a296a2a3a4a2bab3b5a4b7b0a2f8b1b1)**
>  Turtle WoW Team

Dear Turtle WoW team, players, modders, voice actors, and DJs,
I’m just an ordinary gamer who’s been playing Blizzard titles for years. I read your message and saw the examples you gave—Daybreak Game Company, Rockstar Games, NCSoft, Bethesda, Valve, Epic Games, Microsoft, EA, and the Star Wars community. All of them have shown how fan-driven projects can coexist with official IPs. But when it comes to Blizzard/Activision—or now, under Microsoft’s umbrella—I honestly don’t know where Blizzard stands anymore ![😅](//cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/twitter/twemoji@latest/assets/svg/1f605.svg).
As a longtime Diablo II fan, I’ve always felt like Blizzard North was the “forgotten child.” There’s been little innovation, and even less support for the legacy that made Blizzard great. That’s just my opinion, of course—everyone sees things differently, and that’s okay.
I’d like to bring up the example of Dota. Everyone knows it started as a Warcraft III mod. The map creator, IceFrog, didn’t get support from Blizzard, even though the mod was wildly popular. Blizzard didn’t step in or claim it. Instead, Valve said, “If they won’t support you, we will—let’s build Dota 2 together.” And now Dota 2 is one of Valve’s flagship titles.
From the bottom of my heart, I truly hope Blizzard supports your project. But I have serious doubts. Blizzard has long been reluctant to embrace community-driven innovation, and their recent expansions haven’t lived up to the magic of the past. I don’t think they’ll listen to your call… but I hope I’m wrong. I really do. Because the quality and passion behind Turtle WoW deserve recognition—not silence.
Wishing you all the best,
A fellow gamer who still believes in the power of community
content_html:
Dear Blizzard Entertainment,

We're Turtle WoW, a group of fans who love World of Warcraft and share a lifelong dream of contributing to its development. Mysteries of Azeroth, our content expansion, is a collective effort of our community members: writers, developers, 3D-modellers, composers, voice actors, game designers, artists, and radio DJs, each pouring their soul and skills into creating an environment where others can experience the vision we all share through expanding and adding onto the universe you have created.

During the seven years we've been online, we have worked towards finding the right recipe to add an element of replayability to the natural progression of an MMO world. Every update brings fresh areas to explore, new ways to engage with the game, and levelling challenges that require players to approach the experience with creativity and strategy, while the hard‑earned progress they've fought for remains valuable as the game continues to evolve. The response from our community has been nothing short of positive and heart‑warming. Our players have consistently expressed that Mysteries of Azeroth "feels like a home that always welcomes players back".

Many successful games have a modding community. It is a part of gaming culture and a testament to the game's quality, and the community's passion. The World of Warcraft modding community is flourishing, and as more tools become available, it will only continue to grow. Everything your devoted fans create enriches the game universe with diverse perspectives and innovative ideas. Your storytelling has inspired this creativity, and we hope that Blizzard embraces fan‑driven content as its own legacy, rather than alienate this passionate community.

Unfortunately, unlike other studios, Blizzard does not yet have a framework that allows projects like ours to operate without risking legal conflict. With that in mind, we respectfully ask that Blizzard consider establishing a formal ecosystem for licensing fan‑run community servers.

On behalf of our community, we can say that all players would be deeply grateful if you would consider working with fan communities like ours to create a clear, lawful pathway for building upon the legacy of the World of Warcraft universe, with your blessing. By fostering an ecosystem for modders to run their own community servers, Blizzard can continue to oversee and control its progress while encouraging fan-driven innovation. This approach would not only enhance the gameplay experience, but also strengthen the bonds between developers and players, ensuring that World of Warcraft remains a true home for everyone who loves it.

Other successful studios have shown how rewarding a well‑structured community‑server ecosystem can be:
  • Daybreak Game Company provides legal permission for Project 1999, a private server that faithfully recreates the classic EverQuest experience. The partnership is confirmed by an official statement and discussed openly on the project's forums.
  • Rockstar Games / GTA V partnered with the FiveM platform that enables community‑run multiplayer servers that use Rockstar’s GTA V engine while adhering to a licensing agreement that permits custom game modes, role‑playing worlds, and user‑generated content. Over 1 million concurrent players have been reported on FiveM servers, illustrating how a major publisher can safely coexist with a fan‑driven ecosystem while maintaining control over the core IP.
  • NCSoft granted a license to the Homecoming private‑server project for City of Heroes, allowing the community to continue operating the MMO under a clear legal agreement that protects the IP and player accounts.
  • Bethesda has long supported Skyrim mods, providing official tools that have kept the game vibrant for years.
  • Valve opened the Source engine to the public, a decision that birthed enduring titles such as Counter‑Strike and Team Fortress 2.
  • Epic Games introduced Creative Mode in Fortnite, turning players into co‑creators and dramatically boosting engagement. Epic also released the source code for Unreal Tournament 99 to the community, allowing fans to continue development, produce new mods, and distribute classic builds through sites like oldunreal.com, thereby demonstrating that a major publisher can safely coexist with a fan‑run ecosystem.
  • Microsoft / Mojang allows third‑party servers such as Hypixel, Mineplex, and many others to host multiplayer experiences built on the Minecraft engine. These servers operate under a clear licensing regime, generate massive player engagement, and extend the life of the core product while remaining fully compliant with Microsoft’s IP policies.
  • EA / Star Wars Battlefront II cooperated with the community project Kyber to fix server‑side exploits, and its lead engineer later joined EA itself. Although no formal licensing announcement exists, this cooperation illustrates how a publisher and a fan‑run server can work together on security and stability.
These examples illustrate that, when a clear licensing framework and technical safeguards are in place, fan‑run servers can extend a franchise's lifespan, fuel low‑cost innovation, and strengthen the brand, all while respecting the publisher's intellectual‑property and security requirements.

Why it matters to Blizzard?

A licensed framework for fan-run servers would extend World of Warcraft's active audience by bringing back players who have drifted away from the official game in search of niche experiences that mainstream releases can't accommodate. Community‑crafted mods fill those gaps, offering gameplay that appeals to smaller, passionate audiences. This not only keeps the overall player base larger and more diverse, but also gives Blizzard a source of successful concepts that can be identified and integrated into future official content.

We are open to any licensing structure that fits Blizzard's risk‑management and financial guidelines. Should Blizzard wish to move forward, we stand ready to adapt and meet whatever technical, security and data‑privacy standards you require.

Turtle WoW Community

For the past seven years our players have poured countless hours into building characters and stories that make Turtle WoW feel like a living, ever‑changing world. Those memories and progress are priceless to us and to the people who call our servers home. A licensing framework would give them a permanent, protected home, so every character and memory can continue to live on without the fear of being lost.

We look forward to the day you embrace this opportunity and would welcome the chance to begin a dialogue, offering any support needed to bring this program to life.

Thank you for considering our ideas. We hope to find a resolution that will be best for the game and its gamers.

[email protected]
Turtle WoW Team

> **Galendor wrote: Fri Oct 17, 2025 6:57 pm**

> > Can we just stop doing this thing where we pretend like twow is just a free fan server and torta runs it out of the goodness of her heart? It's a big business. Fuck blizzard and copyright in general but I don't like this constant framing twow as just a big fan project.
>
>   Can we stop pretending that 3d artists, landscapers, musicians, painters, programmers should work for free?

The best example is Project 99 which was mentioned in this letter to Blizzard.
Their agreement with Daybreak stipulates that they're not allowed to charge players for anything. Subscriptions, paid services and micro-transactions of any kind are not allowed. They **are** allowed to accept donations, but those donations should only be used to cover server and data costs.
No one forces people to work for free, but if you're working on a fan project based on someone else's intellectual property, you should not expect reimbursement for your services.
This is also true for any fan-made mod or remake of Bethesda's games like Skywind, Morroblivion, Skyblivion or Enderal.
This has always been the standard approach to fan projects: If you want to run a fan project, you do it at your own expense and are not allowed to profit off it, and TWoW does not fit this description.

Microsoft did the same in the 90s to IBM when IBM was selling computers with Linux that were cheaper and had better and more stable OS than Windows. And because Microsoft knew their OS was inferior and they couldn't just make it better and cheaper, the only thing they were able to do to stifle out the competition was to file a class action lawsuit against IBM that nearly bankrupted them, but it succeed in not allowing Linux to flourish.

So company that's so stuck up it's own behind can't possibly make something better anymore. Not in this day and age where big media companies are trying their best to create the most progressive products possible, even if they fail miserably. As long as WoW has veterans with Stockholm Syndrome who will always play Retail no matter how bad is it and how they say are against private servers, Activision/Microsoft/Blizzard have the leverage to believe that no matter how horrible their version of the game is, it will continue to sell well. Just like Windows - it's a monopoly in the OS market, just like how WoW is in the MMORPG market, and no matter how horrible Windows gets, Microsoft don't care about making it worse. The amount of people who will move to Linux or Mac is probably the same that move from Retail to private servers. I still believe that private WoW servers and their players are a drop in the sea of WoW players. Maybe there are 10-20 really big WoW private servers, but the rest are too small and insignificant to even care to file a lawsuit against. And I seriously doubt that if you combine all the WoW private server players they will surpass those who play on the official servers. If the situation was so dire, then Blizzard wouldn't even bother closing down servers.

Another example is NCSoft with Lineage 2, they have closed some private servers, but I think the situation there is more dire, because one server closes and probably 4 new ones launch. So they can't handle it. I think in that regard more Lineage 2 players play on private servers than official servers and it's also important where a game is more popular. Lineage 1 is still popular in Korea, but Lineage 2 is more popular in the West, but there are almost no private servers for either L1 or L2 in Korea, which is their main jurisdiction and in the West they don't have that much power when Lineage 2 is most popular in Russia and they can't touch servers there, except most WoW private servers are not in Russia or China, but in the West and WoW is most popular in the West so they have a reason to be doing something about it.

I think Turtle WoW shouldn't be pleading to Blizzard like I said in my first reply here, but rather wait this out and make sure they can persevere instead. Because making a deal with Blizzard is like making a deal with the devil. After such a deal, Turtle WoW will be completely neutered, it will lose its soul and most people will leave for other servers, I know I will if that happens.

author: Grin
subject: Re: Open Letter to Blizzard Entertainment
content_md:
They need to make a game themselves if they are serious about going down this path as developers and wish to submerge deeper into the world of information technology. This platform was only meant to serve for practice, a "target dummy". The game belong to a place as distant from most here as Captain Kirk and the Enterprise. If this lawsuit is serious than it means that Icarus flew too close to the sun and the wings have started to melt away.
Now, I see two choices. Finding a place to land or struggle with damaged wings to stay above water surface as you fly onward. I believe landing is more suited for the situation at hand since this project was meant for practice. If the realm started out as an official project then I'd advise for the latter but since we are talking about a pirate ship that sailed far and wide... knowing full well that it's treasure belonged to others, the hoard must go to its owners. Otherwise, it meant that this team would take over carrying the Blizzard team's legacy for generations to come when, shall I add, many of the developers are still well and kicking. Not to mention that they have passed down their knowledge overtime. If we wish to show our respect and gratitude then we must have faith and wait until they manage to turn the tides of creation.
I do like the idea of legacy realms but what is way more appealing is to partake in creating something similar that they had at some point in my life. I believe that it is important to make that with people you live in relatively close vicinity. Can't imagine something so magnificient to happen without personal presence. However, Turtle is open world. I do think it is awesome for practice and I may be wrong about this but I find it to be too much of a challenge to do all that online. I mean creating a game or run an mmo realm. U can't sit with the people and drink beer. It'd take you away from the people, dogs, cats and furniture around you to create a game with online presence only.
I enjoyed taking part in this journey in my demented ways. I learnt a lot during this time period and matured, so to say, levelled further. However to tell you straight, I haven't done any raids apart from pugs. I am stuck on the storyline and learning the language. That shows to me just how much effort was put into this program. I realised during this time period that the only way to partake in it is if we strive to create something that rivals it instead of building a copy or reconstructing the original.
To summarise my thoughts, the legacy should be carried by them and those who learnt under them, by the people who share personal relationship with them in one way or the other. Spelling this out fills me with so many emotions I can hardly put them into words without loosing focus. As simple as that, Warcraft belong in their hands. One may be acknowledged into their ranks but is this how you should go about it if you wish to join them? Should you at all join them? Do they need help? Wouldn't they asked for it if they did? We just want to be them. "Do you not have phones?"

author: Qualopec
subject: Re: Open Letter to Blizzard Entertainment
content_md:
I only want to write support to Turtle Devs. You  guys did incredible job, and gave me so much joy.
Your  project has vision, passion, and ambition.
And  I hope there will be some sort of solution, where Blizzard won't meddle with your vision, especially when Blizzard doesn't have their own.

I was playing WoW since late TBC -with breaks sure,  but it was quite a long time still. I paid for expansions and subscriptions. And the longer I played the more miserable experience was. Blizzard didn't lose me because of Turtle.  They lost me long before I was even told about this server.
I don't recognise modern WoW,  it feels like completely different franchise, it lost it's feel and spirit, and we've got - excuse my language- corporate slop instead.

I could go on and on explaining, why I gave up on nu-WoW, but  I will not bore everyone with a textwall. I reached a state of apathy, there is nothing Blizzard can do now that would bring me back to retail.

Turtle WoW reminded me why I fell in love with this franchise. And I really dig lots of their ideas, it makes the world feel larger and bigger. I like how the threats are localised, and we don't see World-ending- doom  looming every year.

If Blizzard would be successful in shutting Turtle down,  they won't get me back. In their situation there will be no financial gain. If you want me to pay for your product, release product that is worth paying for. I'm not a masochist to pay  for stuff that give me nothing but frustration and headaches, Dragonflight was the last time I gave you a chance.  I keep checking forums occasionally, and the same problems keep on repeating  over  and over again, and it seems like Blizzard is deaf to feedback. Ok, go ahead and do whatever I'm not paying for that. I am no longer your target audience.

I also want to write best regards to Turtle community, I was very lucky and met excellent people. You're also part, why this experience was one of a kind.

author: Torta
subject: A Journey's End
content_md:
Hello friends,

They say it's the journey, not the destination. How long must a journey last to be remembered fondly and warmly? We don't know. We only know that ours is coming to an end.

After almost 8 years online, Turtle WoW is heading towards shutdown. The final day of operation will be May 14, 2026, and the servers will go offline at 12:00 AM on May 15th.

Working on Turtle WoW has been the highlight of our lives. It has been an honor to build with you and for you. Whether you were exploring new stories, leveling, raiding, PvPing, roleplaying, or just enjoying a quiet moment in the world, seeing how much this game means to you has been our greatest privilege.

The adventures you had, the battles you fought, and the friends you met are what made it all worthwhile. We hope you will cherish those moments. What we leave behind are fond memories of an 8-year-long journey, and we hope you'll remember it every now and then.

Until the project's final day, we'll keep technical and in-game support active for everyone who keeps playing. All realm timelines will be immediately shifted to the final progression patch for those who want to see the new raids before the project's sunset.

We've turned off all donations until the end of the project and want to thank you sincerely for supporting us over the years.

Our website, forums, and social media will also be closed on October 16th.

Finally, we want to thank our incredible team.

Thank you for playing.

Thank you for being such a wonderful gaming community.

Thank you for your creativity and talent.

Thank you.

 *Turtle WoW*

Sad To read that. I personally hopes for TurtleWoW To stay firm against Blizzard. Especially those outside of Blizzards reach and US jurisdiction.

Nonetheless...

I wanna Take a Moment To thank everyone i came across during my 4+ years here on TurtleWoW. Especially those i had pleasent experiences with out in the open world, in Raids and Dungeons, during Our Times across different Discord Servers.

author: Skurridizo
subject: Re: A Journey's End
content_md:
In the lands of Azeroth,
where the wild winds blow,
a hunter without fear,
too fast for any foe!

He leveled up with nothing
just courage, grit, and pride,
no allies by his side to help,
he still rose up to win the fight.

No epics, just plain gear,
he climbed with daring might,
two fists from Orgrimmar,
his loyal arms ’til end of fight!

With precision as his guide,
no fear will make him fall,
in Zul'Gurub he strikes,
and none can match at all!

The legendary hunter goes
runs through Azeroth world!
His name is Skurridithzo,
his traps a copper glow.
With Chucho the scorpion,
and Broken Tooth, the champion.
Not even Nefarian
nor Ragnaros can stop them!

From Durotar to Plaguelands,

and traps begin to soar!

content_html:
Hello friends,

They say it's the journey, not the destination. How long must a journey last to be remembered fondly and warmly? We don't know. We only know that ours is coming to an end.

After almost 8 years online, Turtle WoW is heading towards shutdown. The final day of operation will be May 14, 2026, and the servers will go offline at 12:00 AM on May 15th.

Working on Turtle WoW has been the highlight of our lives. It has been an honor to build with you and for you. Whether you were exploring new stories, leveling, raiding, PvPing, roleplaying, or just enjoying a quiet moment in the world, seeing how much this game means to you has been our greatest privilege.

The adventures you had, the battles you fought, and the friends you met are what made it all worthwhile. We hope you will cherish those moments. What we leave behind are fond memories of an 8-year-long journey, and we hope you'll remember it every now and then.

Until the project's final day, we'll keep technical and in-game support active for everyone who keeps playing. All realm timelines will be immediately shifted to the final progression patch for those who want to see the new raids before the project's sunset.

We've turned off all donations until the end of the project and want to thank you sincerely for supporting us over the years.

Our website, forums, and social media will also be closed on October 16th.

Finally, we want to thank our incredible team.

Thank you for playing.

Thank you for being such a wonderful gaming community.

Thank you for your creativity and talent.

Thank you.

Turtle WoW

author: Beardozer
subject: Re: A Journey's End
content_md:
I joined Turtle WoW the day I saw the lawsuit filed last year. I figured it was then or never. And I am very glad I did. The experience from this server was the best I have ever had in gaming, both inside wow and out. It was incredible how well the new content was designed. There were bugs, there were glitches, the 1.12 client groaned under the weight of a 20 year old codebase, but the gameplay and content were the best bar none.

Thank you for the 1.18.0 holy paladin. I never thought about a melee healing paladin class before, but it turned out to fit the class fantasy so well. What else would a shield wearing, plate wearing healer class do other than charge in with the tank and heal from close range?

My favorite zone was Northwind. I found my pet Billy there. I didn't know I wanted Billy, but Billy stayed with me throughout the rest of my time in azeroth. We saw MC together, we cleared BWL together, we toured K10 and ZG, all with Billy happily quacking along beside me.

I never thought transmogs or new content belonged in Vanilla. But now I can't imagine playing classic without it. This wasn't Vanilla, but to me it certainly played and felt like vanilla. The stuff added by Turtle felt like it came from the original game and from the original developers. It was awesome how the new content did not remove the old; and the amount of new levelling content was incredible.

Thanks again for the memories. I'll miss you guys, but I'm glad I got in when I did and got a solid 6+ months of experience out of it.

Cheers,

Healdozer
Cartographer
<AARP>

Ambershire

author: Dogfight
subject: Re: A Journey's End
content_md:
Thanks for everything to everyone on the Twow team!
This has been the best WoW experience I've ever had in my 20 years playing it, so that means a lot. A community that rivals the feeling of OG Vanilla and quality class and content development that still kept that Vanilla feeling.

It's a shame this journey comes to an end, but I am not sad. I am happy for all the memories and friends I've made here. I finally got satisfied that hollow feeling I've had from January 2007, that Vanilla had so much more unrealized potential. Through my four years here on Twow I got more than I had hoped for from a Vanilla+ server, it exceeded my expectations.

One thing is for certain; I will never pay to play on Blizzards WoW servers. It will always be a step down from all that Twow has created. And actually having GMs for real interaction makes a huge difference.

It was a blast. Lets enjoy the last few weeks of Twow. Thanks for all the good times!
Thank you.

author: Bobromil519
subject: Re: A Journey's End
content_md:
Hello,

Turtle team, please take a moment to read the following message.

The situation that is now unfolding — not only for you, but also for other competing private servers — represents a significant opportunity. If handled correctly, it can truly be turned to your advantage.

You have managed to create something unique. Something that has been missing from the gaming scene for a long time — and still is. Personally, I do not believe that Blizzard will learn from this or deliver what players truly want.

On the MMORPG scene today, there is no game that has the same “soul” as WoW Classic. And this is exactly what players are missing — and will continue to miss. This creates a massive gap in the market.

And this is where a major opportunity opens up — not just for your team.

Create your own MMORPG.

A game that is not a copy of WoW, but is inspired by it. A game that carries the same soul as WoW Classic. A game without aggressive microtransactions, without excessive flashy effects, one that doesn’t hold the player’s hand, offers real challenge — and most importantly, has character.

You already have a huge advantage: you understand what players want. You know what works. And you don’t need cutting-edge graphics — WoW Classic itself is proof of that.
It is important to realize that in the near future, many private servers will likely shut down.

Players will be frustrated and will be searching for a new “home.” We are not talking about hundreds, but tens of thousands of players worldwide.

If, at that moment, a meaningful and well-designed project appears, it can gain massive community support.
I believe that if you come up with your own MMO project with a clear vision, you could raise significant funding through platforms like Kickstarter or similar. Thousands — even tens of thousands — of people would support you, if the project is handled correctly and offers something truly unique.

And I believe you are capable of that. You have already proven it with Turtle WoW.

You already have a foundation (for example, your work in Unreal Engine) — why not build on it again? Create your own assets, refine the style, and develop a game that does not infringe on copyrights, while still capturing the spirit players love.
The key is to start as soon as possible — while emotions are still strong and the community is active.

Consider reaching out to other teams as well — such as Epoch, Ascension, and developers from similar projects. By joining forces, you could build a strong team capable of creating something truly exceptional.

Right now, many projects are coming to an end — and with that comes a huge pool of people, developers, experience, and know-how. A large number of individuals who share the same mindset and vision as WoW Classic — and who can form a healthy, non-toxic team.

I truly believe that if you create a project inspired by WoW Classic, you will receive massive support from the community. Especially now, when many players are losing their servers and Blizzard is unable to provide a meaningful alternative.
What you have achieved over the past 8 years is incredible.
But this does not have to be the end.

On the contrary — it can be the beginning of something much bigger.

Something of your own, something you can be proud of, without needing to hide.

I believe that if you come together, you can create something truly special. And one day, Blizzard may regret its decision to shut down these projects instead of working with them.
There are games (such as Minecraft) that were created by a very small team and are now popular worldwide.

Why couldn’t you achieve the same? You already have the team — and it can become even bigger.

You are now in a position you can take advantage of. Come together, unite your efforts across the WoW scene, and go for it. People will support you.

Unknown, generic Czech player
Bobromil

We need to be loud and support the team!

And this is where a major opportunity opens up — not just for your team.

Create your own MMORPG.

A game that is not a copy of WoW, but is inspired by it. A game that carries the same soul as WoW Classic. A game without aggressive microtransactions, without excessive flashy effects, one that doesn’t hold the player’s hand, offers real challenge — and most importantly, has character.

You already have a huge advantage: you understand what players want. You know what works. And you don’t need cutting-edge graphics — WoW Classic itself is proof of that.
It is important to realize that in the near future, many private servers will likely shut down.

Players will be frustrated and will be searching for a new “home.” We are not talking about hundreds, but tens of thousands of players worldwide.

If, at that moment, a meaningful and well-designed project appears, it can gain massive community support.
I believe that if you come up with your own MMO project with a clear vision, you could raise significant funding through platforms like Kickstarter or similar. Thousands — even tens of thousands — of people would support you, if the project is handled correctly and offers something truly unique.

And I believe you are capable of that. You have already proven it with Turtle WoW.

You already have a foundation (for example, your work in Unreal Engine) — why not build on it again? Create your own assets, refine the style, and develop a game that does not infringe on copyrights, while still capturing the spirit players love.
The key is to start as soon as possible — while emotions are still strong and the community is active.

Consider reaching out to other teams as well — such as Epoch, Ascension, and developers from similar projects. By joining forces, you could build a strong team capable of creating something truly exceptional.

Right now, many projects are coming to an end — and with that comes a huge pool of people, developers, experience, and know-how. A large number of individuals who share the same mindset and vision as WoW Classic — and who can form a healthy, non-toxic team.

I truly believe that if you create a project inspired by WoW Classic, you will receive massive support from the community. Especially now, when many players are losing their servers and Blizzard is unable to provide a meaningful alternative.
What you have achieved over the past 8 years is incredible.
But this does not have to be the end.

On the contrary — it can be the beginning of something much bigger.

Something of your own, something you can be proud of, without needing to hide.

I believe that if you come together, you can create something truly special. And one day, Blizzard may regret its decision to shut down these projects instead of working with them.
There are games (such as Minecraft) that were created by a very small team and are now popular worldwide.

Why couldn’t you achieve the same? You already have the team — and it can become even bigger.

You are now in a position you can take advantage of. Come together, unite your efforts across the WoW scene, and go for it. People will support you.

author: Safyre
subject: Re: A Journey's End
content_md:
Blizzard's inevitable change after the good workers were gotten rid of, left me bouncing around from game to game and even then, from private realm to realm. The place I found to stay became Turtle WoW Mysteries of Azeroth. Even the glitches were more favorable than Classic WoW from retail. The new content of zones, trade skills, and more were kept in the spirit of the lore and fantastic for as much as I've experienced.

Admittedly, I haven't been able to experience all of it. You see, I never even achieved level 60. I kept spreading word of mouth and was able to create a small guild with those I convinced to move to the Azeroth of the Turtles, Shadows of Valor, a name used to show progression from our Classic WoW guild, The Valiant. And every time I got a new player to join, I had to make a new character to play with them until they could 'catch up'.

This news makes me extremely sad. Turtle WoW is my escape and one of the only games that I can play and not really complain about. There will now be a huge void in my being.

I don't know how close you could keep a similar game to keep the feel and enjoyment of TWoW, but I can really hope that it happens. Change names, change some art, create custom assets, remodel the terrain, etc. and keep on going? Is that possible? I can only hope something like that happens. Or maybe the legal stuff says not to even continue with the genre, or any game at all.

I can only hope something better, bigger, and more enjoyable comes from this.
Thank you for all the work you've put into this game and the enjoyment you've brought to me and many others.

author: Alchemister
subject: Navigating the injunction through jurisdictional relocation
content_md:
turtle_tongue  **Dear Team and Community,**

With the recent legal developments and the pressure from Blizzard’s legal counsel, it is clear that continuing operations under the current jurisdiction has become untenable. However, I believe there is a viable path forward to preserve the project’s legacy through jurisdictional arbitrage.

As of 2026, the legal landscape in the Russian Federation provides a unique "legal sanctuary" for digital projects facing IP-related litigation from "unfriendly jurisdictions" (specifically the US and EU). By establishing a localized legal entity and migrating the infrastructure to Russian-based data centers, the project would effectively become immune to the current permanent injunction issued by the US District Court.

- following the precedent set by Government Decree No. 299, which reduces compensation for IP holders from "unfriendly" nations to 0%, the Russian legal environment has become effectively immune to copyright claims from these jurisdictions. This creates a solid "safe haven" for projects that would otherwise be suppressed by DMCA or US-based permanent injunctions.
- any attempt by Blizzard to pursue legal action within the Russian court system would be met with years of procedural delays, high costs, and a high probability of dismissal based on national interests.
- given that the team already has trusted Russian-speaking staff (GMs), the logistical transition regarding management and localization would be significantly mitigated.

While this may introduce challenges regarding latency for certain regions and necessitate a shift in payment processing, it is the only guaranteed way to prevent a total sunset of the project.

I urge the administration to consider this "safe haven" approach before the May 14th deadline. The code and the community are too valuable to be surrendered to corporate litigation.

content_html:
Dear Team and Community,

With the recent legal developments and the pressure from Blizzard’s legal counsel, it is clear that continuing operations under the current jurisdiction has become untenable. However, I believe there is a viable path forward to preserve the project’s legacy through jurisdictional arbitrage.

As of 2026, the legal landscape in the Russian Federation provides a unique "legal sanctuary" for digital projects facing IP-related litigation from "unfriendly jurisdictions" (specifically the US and EU). By establishing a localized legal entity and migrating the infrastructure to Russian-based data centers, the project would effectively become immune to the current permanent injunction issued by the US District Court.
  • following the precedent set by Government Decree No. 299, which reduces compensation for IP holders from "unfriendly" nations to 0%, the Russian legal environment has become effectively immune to copyright claims from these jurisdictions. This creates a solid "safe haven" for projects that would otherwise be suppressed by DMCA or US-based permanent injunctions.
  • any attempt by Blizzard to pursue legal action within the Russian court system would be met with years of procedural delays, high costs, and a high probability of dismissal based on national interests.
  • given that the team already has trusted Russian-speaking staff (GMs), the logistical transition regarding management and localization would be significantly mitigated.
While this may introduce challenges regarding latency for certain regions and necessitate a shift in payment processing, it is the only guaranteed way to prevent a total sunset of the project.

I urge the administration to consider this "safe haven" approach before the May 14th deadline. The code and the community are too valuable to be surrendered to corporate litigation.

author: Alchemister
subject: Re: Navigating the injunction through jurisdictional relocation
content_md:
> **Hoo wrote: Mon Apr 20, 2026 7:48 pm**
> This indeed sounded solid a year ago, but today the risk of Ru net going full china mode has risen dramatically. It is ofc a matter of much debate going on in our government, but nevertheless more and more preparations for this to *become possible* are getting set in place each month. And at the end of the day Putin's word would be final if he orders such.
>  ...still it might be worth a gamble, worst case scenario such new project might turn to russian/chinese access only XD

While the "sovereign internet" narrative is a popular talking point, the technical and economic reality of 2026 tells a different story. The concerns about a "full China-style" isolation of the Russian segment are largely based on a misunderstanding of the infrastructure's purpose.

Here is why the "isolation" argument doesn't hold water for a project like this:

- the legislative and technical preparations (like the Sovereign Internet Law) are designed to create a defensive segment for state infrastructure, critical industries, and the banking sector. It is about "autonomy" in case of external disconnection, not "isolation" by choice. No credible strategic roadmap suggests a total decoupling from the global web, as it would be equivalent to economic suicide.
- the Russian economy in 2026 is deeply integrated into global supply chains through "friendly" and neutral jurisdictions. Modern commerce, even when localized, relies on global IP routing, BGP stability, and cross-border data flows. A total "whitelist" approach would collapse the remaining private sector overnight. The government is well aware that commerce cannot survive, let alone rebuild, in a vacuum.
- even in the most restrictive scenarios, gaming traffic is rarely the target of state-level blocking unless it carries specific political content. For a server like Turtle WoW, the risk is minimal because the project doesn't interfere with national security. In fact, hosting international projects provides a degree of "soft power" and attracts foreign currency, which is beneficial to the local digital economy.
- a transition to a truly isolated intranet would require a complete overhaul of the national backbone, which would take at least a decade of stable development. In the current volatile environment, the priority is connectivity, not isolation.

IMHO: moving the server to Russia isn't a gamble on "if the door closes," but rather a strategic move to a jurisdiction where the Western legal "keys" (lawsuits/DMCA) no longer fit the lock. The door to the global internet will remain open because Russia's own economy depends on it.

author: Mircea001
subject: Re: A Journey's End
content_md:
It’s hard to put into words what the recent news means for all of us. Eight years of history, world-building, and community are coming to a close, and it truly feels like the end of an era.

To the Developers: Thank you for creating a place where we could truly lose ourselves in adventure again. You gave me some of the most intense moments I’ve ever experienced in a game. I will never forget being level 40 on my Hardcore Warlock, sprinting through the Ruins of Alterac with three Elite Ogres on my heels  jumping over a wall with my heart racing and escaping with only 10 HP left out of 1K. It’s those 'heart-in-your-throat' moments that made Turtle WoW so special, and I’m grateful for every single one of them.

To the Community: It has been an honor to level, trade, and survive alongside you. Whether we met in a random camp or a high-level raid, you made this world feel like home.

As we approach May 15th, part of me is still holding onto a bit of 'Hardcore' hope. I keep imagining a final announcement where you guys suddenly pull a 'Wolf of Wall Street' move, grab the mic, and scream: 'WE’RE NOT FCKING LEAVING! THE SHOW GOES ON!'* But even if the sun does set on this project, thank you for the ride of a lifetime. It was a privilege to be part of the Turtle WoW family.

Slow and steady... until the end.

Ridiculously dangerously addictive hooks. These helped me outwit my own miscoded brain which fortunately resulted in this being the last part of WoW I choose to partake in. Thank you for helping me kill my desire or rather need to procrastinate, to put off actual tasks into the future because they felt like a chore. When it started to be said that the end of turtle was reached and shutdown awaited, I came to the realization that this is not really something I need, but rather chose to take part. Probably due to immaturity and laziness. Time to step up and say goodbye to videogames!

author: Samwyse
subject: Re: A Journey's End
content_md:
There are so many emotions in a situation like this, Anger, Regret, remorse, did I mention Anger?  Appreciation I'd like to express to the Dev and GM teams...to basically the entire Turtle WoW team. What you created here for us and in part of course for yourselves....I mean WHO doesn't like playing on Turtle WoW? These servers have been an absolute eye opener into a World I had missed because of timing with another game by Sony that was taken away. I played WoW first half way through Cata, me and my family all 3 of use, to which became 4 and then more but the point is, we ALL missed the beginning of what was to become another mystifiying experience based not just in the graphics of a game but rooted more in the Community it served. Turtle showed me and again my family what it was we missed in those classic WoW days but more importantly again....a caring and helpful and engaging Community.  I will remember begging for an Ony Buff standing most times with my friend who I met right there at the gates to SW named Rusty. We never did anything except sit there waiting for a buff, and we seldom talked other than to say hi, even when we might be on alts, we just KNEW it was the other person. I will always think fondly of that.  Thanks Rusty, it was cool my HC Gnome only having friend. Good luck and Good bye bud.    And, while I sit here and wipe away a wistful tear, Thats the kind of thing that Blizzard/Activision can NEVER take away.   Again, Thank you Turtle WoW, you WILL be missed, but NEVER forgotten.

Most lovingly,
Samwyse Gamgee

> **Vazhieran wrote: Thu Apr 23, 2026 6:34 pm**
> Turtle WoW deserves the Warcraft IP more than Blizzard.
>
>
>  Is there any way they can take this to court and argue that the initial devs no longer work on it so it should be free reign? Why should Microsoft be allowed to keep an IP they never worked on? What have they done for Warcraft recently that justifies them keeping it?

I'm not sure on the precise details of Modern Copyright law, but I'm pretty sure it just protects the owner for a set period of ~90 years I think? The only reason it's been extended so much (The original law only protected it for a period of 14 years in the copyright act of 1790) is because Disney wants to own their IP forever.

I'm sure any romantic could argue that Blizzard ought to lose the right to their IP for their blatant lack of any care for it whatsoever, but the problem is that won't hold up in court before the law and Lawyers famously do not have Souls.

If it were up to me I'd say IP and Copyright should last for ~20 years or so before the property becomes Public Domain with which anyone can spin it anyway they want. However the Rich Corporations will never let that become the law because it'll force them to actually innovate or compete with their fans which Microsoft has consistently proven they cannot do.

TLDR: Copyright Law is Ass, Fuck Activision-MicroSlop-Blizzard. I will not for a million years let a single dime of mine fall into their greedy clutches. I suppose this is the end of my interest in WoW until another Private Server gets my attention.

Fare thee well Turtle WoW and Tel' Abim. It was a fun Journey while it lasted.
